report.message:
The symptoms match patterns from past cloud object-store and metadata-service incidents. Below are the most likely causes, ranked by confidence, based on the available post-mortems.

### Operational or configuration change affecting an object-store subsystem (confidence: medium)

**What happened:** In DAN-104, a command issued with a typo removed too many S3 servers, including the index subsystem (metadata and location of all S3 objects) and the placement subsystem (allocation of new storage), making all GET, LIST, PUT, and DELETE requests fail across the region and cascading to EC2, EBS snapshot-backed volumes, Lambda, and the S3 console. In DAN-036, a configuration change intended to reduce metadata storage load instead overloaded the blob lookup system, triggering a cascading failure across dependent blob-storage services. Both match the current incident because a cloud object store is failing across every API in a region and cascading to dependent compute, volume, function, control-panel, and status services.

**How it was fixed:** The S3 index subsystem was restarted so GET, LIST, and DELETE could resume, then the placement subsystem was restarted so PUT could resume (DAN-104). The job making configuration changes was stopped to recover from the cascading failure (DAN-036).

**How to prevent it:** Modify capacity-removal tools to remove capacity more slowly and add safeguards to prevent capacity from being removed when it will take any subsystem below its minimum required capacity level; audit other operational tools for similar safety checks; make changes to improve recovery time of key S3 subsystems; refactor services into smaller cells to reduce blast radius (DAN-104). Improve ability to quickly provision resources to recover from cascading failures; add software measures to prevent configuration changes that overload key parts of the system; improve load shedding behavior of the metadata storage system so it degrades gracefully under overload (DAN-036).

**Sources:** [Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/41926/), [Google Cloud Storage Incident #19002](https://status.cloud.google.com/incident/storage/19002)

### Regional network disruption overloading the metadata service (confidence: medium)

**What happened:** In DAN-109, a network disruption caused many storage servers to simultaneously request membership data from the metadata service; the metadata service was under such high load that it could not respond within time limits, storage nodes failed to complete membership renewal, became unavailable, and kept retrying, which maintained high load on the metadata service and caused other storage nodes to become unavailable too. This matches the current incident because it involves an object store with storage nodes and a metadata service failing region-wide across all APIs and cascading to dependent services.

**How it was fixed:** Requests to the metadata service were paused to decrease retry activity and relieve load. Significant capacity was then added to the metadata service. Requests were reactivated and storage servers were put back into the customer request path.

**How to prevent it:** Significantly increase the capacity of the metadata service; instrument stricter monitoring on performance dimensions such as membership size; reduce the rate at which storage nodes request membership data; lengthen the time allowed to process queries; segment the DynamoDB service so it has many instances of the metadata service, each serving only portions of the storage server fleet.

**Source:** [Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption and Related Impacts in the US-East Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/5467D2/)

### DNS automation race condition emptying the regional endpoint record (confidence: low)

**What happened:** In DAN-075, a latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management left the regional endpoint record empty: two DNS Enactor processes raced, a second Enactor applied a newer plan and ran cleanup while the first overwrote the regional endpoint with a stale older plan, and the cleanup process then deleted that older plan, removing all IP addresses so clients could not resolve the service APIs. This could explain the current incident because a corrupted or emptied regional object-store endpoint record would make every object API request fail across the region and cascade to VMs, functions, and control-plane services.

**How it was fixed:** The available post-mortem does not describe the specific steps used to restore the DNS endpoint during the incident.

**How to prevent it:** Fix the race condition scenario and add additional protections to prevent the application of incorrect DNS plans; add a velocity control mechanism to limit the capacity a single NLB can remove when health check failures cause AZ failover; build an additional test suite to augment EC2 scale testing for the DWFM recovery workflow; improve the throttling mechanism in EC2 data propagation systems to rate limit incoming work based on the size of the waiting queue.

**Source:** [Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/101925/)

## What to check now
- Whether any operational command or configuration change was issued shortly before the failure.
- Which internal object-store subsystem failed (index, placement, blob lookup, metadata service, DNS endpoint, etc.).
- Error messages or logs from the failing APIs to distinguish between metadata overload, DNS resolution failure, or subsystem restart.
- Whether the status-page notice failure is because the status page itself depends on the object store or because a separate control-plane subsystem is also down.
- DNS resolution for the regional object-store endpoint.
- Metadata service load and storage node membership or renewal status.

report.message:
The symptoms point to a Redis or backing data store failure cascading through your messaging service, similar to past incidents involving Discord, Cloudflare, and Slack. No change was mentioned before the failure, so the exact trigger is not confirmed.

### Redis primary node failover mishandled by API instances (confidence: medium)

**What happened:** In DAN-145, GCP automatically migrated a Redis primary node, which incorrectly dropped offline and forced a cluster rebalance. Discord API instances did not handle the Redis failover correctly, degrading the API service and cascading into a full real-time system failure with clients reconnecting en masse.

**How it was fixed:** Engineers executed a rolling restart of all API instances, corrected an improperly configured API setting for an expensive route, and modified the cached route behavior to handle errors without degrading other services.

**How to prevent it:** Increase the priority of fixing known Redis failover issues; add monitoring around signals that would alert to a cascading failure early; continue improving overall reliability and failure handling of affected services.

**Source:** [Discord Status - Unavailable Guilds & Connection Issues](https://status.discordapp.com/incidents/qk9cdgnqnhcn)

### Backing data store failure cascading to dependent workers (confidence: medium)

**What happened:** In DAN-139, a third-party cloud provider backing Workers KV failed, causing a complete outage for cold reads and writes. In DAN-222, a Cassandra cluster crashed, producers blocked on queue insert operations, and the entire application failed.

**How it was fixed:** DAN-139 teams cut over critical KV namespaces to their own infrastructure and removed dependency on any single provider. DAN-222 broke the dependency between the queue feeding Cassandra and other subsystems, flushed buffered data through other subsystems, and rebuilt a new Cassandra cluster with upgraded software.

**How to prevent it:** Avoid singular dependencies on storage infrastructure you do not own; add short-term blast-radius remediations for individual products; implement tooling to progressively re-enable namespaces during storage infrastructure issues; add greater separation for real-time pipelines; break queueing dependencies so one failing subsystem does not take down others.

**Sources:**
- [Cloudflare - Cloudflare service outage June 12, 2025](https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-service-outage-june-12-2025/)
- [Stackdriver - Report on October 23 Stackdriver Outage](https://www.stackdriver.com/post-mortem-october-23-stackdriver-outage/)

### Deployment or configuration change bug in workers (confidence: low)

**What happened:** In DAN-217, an automation malfunction deployed corrupted code to web servers and job queue workers, disconnecting users. The simultaneous reconnections overwhelmed database capacity and caused cascading connection failures.

**How it was fixed:** Slack added additional database capacity and made optimizations to reconnection methods to reduce the capacity needed during mass disconnection-reconnection events.

**How to prevent it:** The post-mortem we have does not describe a separate prevention checklist beyond the immediate fixes above.

**Source:** [Slack - This was not normal. Really.](https://web.archive.org/web/20181208123409/https://slackhq.com/this-was-not-normal-really)

**What to check now**
- Redis cluster logs and whether a node failover or migration occurred
- API worker error messages for Redis connection timeouts, authentication, or other failures
- Whether a deployment or configuration change went out before the failures
- Whether the unhealthy hosting worker and the strange session workers share the same root cause
- What the "costly API operation" is and whether clients are hammering it

report.message:
The Consul symptoms you described match patterns seen in past incidents. Below are the ranked hypotheses, from most to least likely.

### Consul streaming feature rollout increased cluster load (confidence: medium)

**What happened:** In the Roblox incident, enabling Consul streaming on a traffic-routing service—and adding 50 percent more nodes—was followed by high CPU contention on Consul servers, slow KV writes, and Raft members falling behind. Your incident shows the same Consul symptoms: KV updates taking seconds instead of milliseconds, elevated CPU on a single host, followers lagging, and the primary losing sync with voting peers. The difference is that no recent change was reported before your degradation started.

**How it was fixed:** Roblox disabled the Consul streaming feature for all Consul systems, including the traffic-routing nodes. The config change finished propagating at 15:51, after which Consul p50 latency improved.

**Changes:** Disabled the Consul streaming feature via configuration change.

**How to prevent it:** Remove the circular dependency between telemetry and Consul. Extend telemetry for better visibility into Consul and BoltDB performance. Add targeted alerts when the system approaches the outage state. Extend visibility into traffic patterns between services and Consul.

Source: [Roblox - Roblox Return to Service | Roblox](https://blog.roblox.com/2022/01/roblox-return-to-service-10-28-10-31-2021/)

### BoltDB free-page fragmentation from Consul snapshots (confidence: medium)

**What happened:** Consul uses BoltDB for its Raft log. Snapshots delete the oldest log entries, but BoltDB never shrinks on disk; deleted pages are marked free and reused. Roblox’s workload exposed a pathological BoltDB freelist performance issue that made leaders slow. This matches your slow KV writes, members falling behind, and the primary losing synchronization. The post-mortem notes the root cause was only determined after the outage, and your incident has no known snapshot or disk-growth trigger.

**How it was fixed:** The provided post-mortem passages do not describe a specific fix for the BoltDB fragmentation issue.

**Changes:** None described in the available text.

**How to prevent it:** The provided post-mortem passages do not describe specific prevention steps for this issue.

Source: [Roblox - Roblox Return to Service | Roblox](https://blog.roblox.com/2022/01/roblox-return-to-service-10-28-10-31-2021/)

### Service-discovery quorum loss from a thundering herd (confidence: low)

**What happened:** In the Datadog incident, recycling a smaller cluster caused a sudden surge of DNS requests to the service discovery system. The cluster lost quorum, could not reliably register or deregister services, and failed to answer requests, causing downstream applications to fail. This shares the service-discovery and downstream health-check failure pattern, but your incident also reports slow KV writes and single-host CPU elevation, which the Datadog passage does not describe.

**How it was fixed:** The service discovery team stabilized the cluster by cutting it off from all clients and controlling re-admission; adding more capacity did not help because consensus systems need a quorum.

**Changes:** None described in the available text.

**How to prevent it:** The provided post-mortem passages do not contain a specific prevention checklist for this failure mode.

Source: [Datadog - 2020-09-25 Incident: Infrastructure connectivity issue impacting multiple systems | Datadog](https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/2020-09-25-infrastructure-connectivity-issue/)

**What to check now**
- Whether Consul streaming was recently enabled or changed.
- BoltDB disk usage and snapshot activity on the Consul hosts.
- Which host has elevated CPU and whether it is the Consul leader.
- Consul logs for Raft term changes, snapshot errors, or slow-leader warnings.

The symptoms match patterns seen in past incidents where groups of servers dropped together. No single cause is confirmed, but the closest match is a latent bug triggered by an internal database data update.

### A data update to an internal database triggered a latent bug in the advertising gateway servers (confidence: medium)
What happened: In DAN-116, a data update from an internal database triggered an old double-free bug in the impression bus servers, which receive ad requests, conduct auctions and serve winning ads. All impbus servers worldwide crashed at nearly the same time, halting ad serving. This matches the current incident: the advertising gateway accepts requests, runs bidding/auctions and serves ads, and groups of servers are dropping together.
How it was fixed: Engineering restarted the servers worldwide and restored capacity using a new snapshot from the internal database that was tested and shown not to trigger the bug. They then deployed the updated impbus with the fix.
How to prevent it: Change validation systems so data changes pass only after the deferred deletion time window passes; add a second tier of validation that tests data changes under production traffic; review software testing for corner cases; re-engineer recovery and deployment processes.
Source: [AppNexus - 2013–09–17 Outage Postmortem. On September 17, 2013 starting at 17:54… | by Xandr Engineering | Xandr-Tech | Medium](https://web.archive.org/web/20250505112812/https://medium.com/xandr-tech/2013-09-17-outage-postmortem-586b19ae4307)

### A backend migration or autoscaler behavior shut down groups of gateway servers at once (confidence: medium)
What happened: DAN-115 describes a cell management system that misinterpreted delayed status messages as host failures and started a redistribution storm; DAN-209 describes an autoscaler that unexpectedly turned back on during a Zookeeper migration and shut down servers. Both involve groups of hosts being taken down simultaneously by migration/autoscaler behavior, matching the current symptom. Neither post-mortem describes an advertising gateway or bidding/creative delivery, and the current analyst mentions no migration or autoscaler change.
How it was fixed: In DAN-115, engineers shed load by reducing incoming stream volume from less time-sensitive workloads, added capacity to the secure-connection provisioning subsystem, and changed connection limits. In DAN-209, service was restored after the migration completed.
How to prevent it: Make the autoscaler less aggressive by limiting how many servers can be shut down at once; have two engineers pair during risky parts of migrations; properly disable package management systems during migrations; improve the cell management system to better manage the workload that triggered the issue.

### A database cluster failure or failover problem took down the backend (confidence: low)

The current incident matches a past PostgreSQL primary/replica outage: the replica lagged until synchronization ceased because WAL segments were removed from the primary, database copying attempts stalled, and a configuration change prevented Postgres from starting due to excessive semaphore allocation.

### Configuration change breaking WAL retention and replication slots (confidence: high)

**What happened:** In DAN-164, a spike in database load caused the primary to remove WAL segments before the replica could replicate them, stopping replication. This matches the current incident: the replica lagged until synchronization ceased because the transaction logs it needed were no longer on the main server, fresh database copying attempts stalled, a replication slot shortage was reported, and a configuration change left the database unable to start due to excessive semaphore allocation.

**How it was fixed:** The post-mortem says engineers temporarily increased `max_wal_senders` from the default value of `3` to `32` to allow enough replication connections. When applying the settings, PostgreSQL refused to restart, claiming too many semaphores were being created.

**How to prevent it:** The post-mortem's recovery improvements include:
- Set PostgreSQL's `max_connections` to a sane value
- Investigate Point in time recovery & continuous archiving for PostgreSQL
- Take hourly LVM snapshots of the production databases
- Run automated testing of recovering PostgreSQL database backups
- Improve PostgreSQL replication documentation and runbooks
- Investigate pgbarman for creating PostgreSQL backups
- Investigate using WAL-E for database backup and realtime replication
- Build streaming database restore

Source: [Gitlab - Postmortem of database outage of January 31](https://about.gitlab.com/2017/02/10/postmortem-of-database-outage-of-january-31/)

**What to check now**
- The exact configuration change made right before the failure (WAL retention, max_wal_senders, shared memory/semaphores, or replication slot settings)

Add technical guardrails to ensure all configuration management follows your pipeline. Establish better protocols for implementing and testing WAF rules before production. Add monitoring specifically for WAF behavior and traffic patterns. Investigate organization-wide SCPs restricting IAM roles.

report.message:
The symptoms point to cascading load in the media metadata stack: database pressure, failing media-description lookups, and cache hosts going offline. Three past-incident patterns match, with the strongest being metadata-service overload and cache-layer loss.

### Configuration change or load spike overloaded the metadata database and lookup layer (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-036, a configuration change meant to reduce resource usage overloaded the blob lookup system and triggered a cascading failure across dependent services. In DAN-121, BBC Online’s metadata database became overloaded, throttled requests, and services without local cache began timing out and failing. This mirrors the current incident, where media-description calls fail and the database is under intense pressure.

**How it was fixed:** Google stopped the job making configuration changes and manually reduced load to recover from the cascading failure. BBC restored the caching layer and performed significant remedial work on the metadata service.

**How to prevent it:** Improve resource provisioning speed; prevent configuration changes from overloading key system parts; improve load shedding so the metadata storage system degrades gracefully under overload. BBC also planned to complete forensics and put measures in place to minimize recurrence.

**Source:** [Google Cloud Status Dashboard — A configuration change intended to address an uptick in demand for metadata storage, which overloaded part of the...](https://status.cloud.google.com/incident/storage/19002), [BBC Online outage on Saturday 19th July 2014](https://www.bbc.co.uk/blogs/internet/entries/a37b0470-47d4-3991-82bb-a7d5b8803771)

### Cache-host failure or cluster rebalance removed the caching layer (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-145, an automatic migration of a Redis primary caused it to drop offline, forcing a cluster rebalance that exposed failover bugs and a cache misconfiguration, which cascaded into a full outage. In DAN-109, a network disruption overloaded metadata services, causing storage nodes to take themselves down and retry, which kept load high. This matches the current cache hosts going offline independently and the application tier hitting the database directly.

**How it was fixed:** Discord performed a rolling restart of API instances and later a full service restart, corrected an improperly configured API setting, and modified the behavior of an improperly cached route. Amazon paused requests to the metadata service, added capacity, and reactivated requests once load was under control.

**How to prevent it:** Fix known Redis failover issues; modify cached routes to handle errors without degrading other services; add monitoring for cascading-failure signals. Amazon increased metadata-service capacity, added stricter monitoring, reduced the rate at which storage nodes request membership data, lengthened query processing time, and planned to segment the service.

**Source:** [Discord Status - Unavailable Guilds & Connection Issues](https://status.discordapp.com/incidents/qk9cdgnqnhcn), [Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption and Related Impacts in the US-East Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/5467D2/)

### Slow database or connection-pool constraint created query backups (confidence: low)
**What happened:** In DAN-133, slow MongoDB queries coincided with a JVM upgrade that shrank thread and connection pools, constraining throughput and causing workflow and API backups. This matches the current database pressure and application-tier errors, though the current incident does not mention a JVM upgrade.

**How it was fixed:** CircleCI failed over to healthy MongoDB hosts, restarted slow processes, eliminated unnecessary operations, pulled subsets of fields, disabled Docker detection, tuned thread and connection pools, scaled up MongoDB, and scaled service instances.

**How to prevent it:** Refactor data storage and access patterns; improve observability of database degradation; take corrective action on leading indicators to minimize customer impact.

**Source:** [Postmortem: March 26 - April 10 Workflow Delay Incidents - Announcements - CircleCI Discuss](https://discuss.circleci.com/t/postmortem-march-26-april-10-workflow-delay-incidents/30060)
